editorial_contributions.text: A long knot is a ``knotted line'' which agrees with a regular line outside some 3-ball; a long knot diagram with virtual crossings is a long virtual knot diagram. Long virtual knots have some interesting properties not shared by their compact counterparts. In this paper, the author defines a quandle enhanced with an invertible unary operation which distributes over the usual quandle operation, called a virtual quandle. A set with two virtual quandle structures which satisfy a certain compatibility condition is called a long quandle. Like ordinary quandles and compact knots, long quandles are a source of invariants for long knots. A finite virtual quandle defines a representation of the long knot monoid. An easily computable invariant is described which distinguishes classical long knots from virtual long knots. Long quandles may also be useful for defining new invariants of compact virtual knots.

editorial_contributions.text: The \(\Xi\)-polynomial is a modification of the Jones polynomial with values in a \(\mathbb{Z}[t^{\pm 1}]\)-module over a set of equivalence classes of curves immersed in surfaces. A virtual knot diagram corresponds to a knot diagram drawn on a surface (see [\textit{J. S. Carter, S. Kamada, M. Saito}, J. Knot Theory Ramifications 11, No.~3, 311--322 (2002; Zbl 1004.57007)]); if, in the state-sum expansion of the Kauffman bracket, we carry along the equivalence class of the surface and its embedded curves, we obtain the \(\Xi\)-polynomial. For classical knots, the \(\Xi\)-polynomial is simply the Jones polynomial times the empty set of curves on a sphere, but for virtual knots the invariant contains new information. Some examples of computation of the invariant are given.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: In this work, we construct a generalization of the $G_n^k$-theory to the case of an arbitrary hypergraph. The case of spherical braids is considered separately, using the stratification of the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_n(S^2)$ and the hypergraph $Γ_n^{\mathrm{sph}}$ encoding projective constraints. In contrast to the original $G_{n}^{k}$ theory, where codimension-one properties are determined by exactly $k$ particles, the present work considers various cases corresponding to strata of codimension~$1$. These groups admit nice maps to free products of cyclic groups. Among unsolved problems, we emphasize the question how the above construction works for abelian varieties and, in particular, for elliptic curves.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We introduce a broad family of groups $G(Γ)$ associated with transverse stratifications of moduli spaces. For a wide class of stratifications satisfying a natural local condition (transverse niceness), we construct a homomorphism from the fundamental group of the moduli space to the corresponding group $G(Γ)$. This general theorem, which is proved in the companion paper \cite{Manturov2026}, provides a far-reaching generalization of the $G_n^k$-theory. The main goal of the present paper is to discuss numerous examples and situations where the transverse niceness property actually occurs. We describe various moduli spaces and stratifications that are transversely nice. In particular, we study the hierarchy of configuration spaces of points in the plane defined by algebraic curves and establish the transversality property for conic configurations. The general hierarchy problem is formulated in the final section.

editorial_contributions.text:
This book is an introduction to knot theory, consisting of six parts and appendices.

 Part I. After some basic definitions of links are given, the following link invariants are introduced: linking numbers, Arf invariant, \(3\)-colorings of diagrams, the fundamental group of link exteriors, knot quandles, Conway algebras, the polynomial invariants of Alexander-Conway, Jones, HOMFLY and Kauffman, Khovanov's categorification of the Jones polynomial.

 Part II studies braids. Four definitions of the braid group are given and proved to be equivalent. Other material in this part are: Ocneanu's definition of the HOMFLY polynomial using braid closure, the Burau and the Krammer-Bigelow representations, algorithms for realization of a knot as a braid closure by Alexander and Vogel, algorithms for braid recognition by Artin and Dehornoy, spherical and cylindrical braids, Markov's theorem on braid closure, Makanin's version of Markov's theorem involving unary braids, the Yang-Baxter equation.

 Part III studies Vassiliev's knot invariants. After the usual definition of Vassiliev invariants involving singular knots is given, it is shown that the Vassiliev invariants as a whole are stronger than polynomial invariants. The spaces of chord diagrams and Feynman diagrams are introduced. The bialgebra structure of the space of Feynman diagrams, the relationships between the \(so(3)\)-evaluation of Feynman diagrams and the four-color theorem by Bar-Natan, estimates of the dimensions of the space of chord diagrams, the Kontsevich integral and Goussarov's theorem on arrow diagrams are presented.

 Part IV presents the author's work on atoms, \(d\)-diagrams, bracket semigroups and quasitoric braids. The author gives a proof using \(d\)-diagrams of a theorem by Kauffman and Murasugi on the difference of the highest and the lowest degrees of the Jones polynomial of links.

 Part V studies virtual knots and links. After the usual definition of virtual links involving virtual crossings, the correspondence between virtual links and the stable equivalence class of links in closed, connected, oriented surface is stated. The Gauss diagram approach to virtual links by Goussarov, Polyak and Viro is sketched. The following invariants of virtual links are introduced: fundamental group, Kauffman quandle, Kauffman bracket, the \(VA\)-polynomial, two-variable polynomials and multivariable polynomial, generalized Jones-Kauffman polynomial. Long virtual knots and virtual braids are also studied.

 Part VI studies knots in the real projective \(3\)-space, Kirby's calculus on framed links, the Witten invariant of \(3\)-manifolds, virtual \(3\)-manifolds, and Legendrian knots.

 Appendices contain the independence of the three Reidemeister moves, finite type invariants of virtual links, energy of a knot, a list of unsolved problems, and table of knots up to 10 crossings in Rolfsen's numbering.

 The book presents a large amount of topics in knot theory, including many recent developments. As a consequence, the proofs are sometimes omitted or left as exercises.

title.title: Knot theory

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(D\) be a knot diagram of a virtual knot. That is, \(D\) is a plane 4-valent graph which is the image in the plane of an immersion of a number of oriented circles (the components) in general position. Each vertex is designated a positive or negative classical or virtual crossing in the usual way. There is also the possibility that the positive and negative crossings are equalized and we have a diagram of a flat virtual knot.

Suppose now that the number of components is one. A classical crossing is said to be even (odd) if on transversing the knot from the crossing until it returns, the number of classical crossings encountered is even (odd). Alternatively in the chord diagram, the chord corresponding to the crossing passes an even (odd) number of other chords. The properties satisfied by the parity are the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item[1.] If \(X\) is a vertex of a monogon, i.e. obtained by a Reidemeister I move, then \(X\) is even.
\item[2.] Both crossings created by a Reidemeister 2 move have the same parity.
\item[3.] Let crossings \(X_1\), \(X_2\), \(X_3\) transform to \(Y_1\), \(Y_2\), \(Y_3\) under a Reidemeister 3 move. Then
\begin{itemize}
\item[a)] corresponding crossings have the same parity,
\item[b)] the number of odd crossings is 0 or 2.
\end{itemize}
\item[4.] Any crossings not involved in a Reidemeister move keep their parity.
\end{itemize}
1., 2. and 3a) are easy to see. 3b) follows because a triangle meets a line in 0 or 2 points. Alternatively the integer equations 
\[
x= a+ b,\;y= b+c,\;z= c+ a
\]
 only have 0 or 2 odd solutions.
A classical diagram with no virtual crossings has all its crossings even. It follows that a diagram with an odd number of odd vertices cannot represent a classical knot.

In this paper the author defines 1. to 4. above as the parity axioms and gives some examples of parities.

For example let \({\mathcal D}\) be the set of virtual diagrams and let \({\mathcal D}_\infty\) be those with all crossings even. So \({\mathcal D}_\infty\) contains all classical diagrams.

There is a map from \({\mathcal D}\) to \({\mathcal D}_\infty\) obtained by repeatedly replacing odd vertices by virtual ones.

There is a parity defined on crossings in \({\mathcal D}_\infty\) as follows. Let \(c(X)\) be the chord in the chord diagram of \(D\) with direction going from the overcrossing point to the undercrossing point. The index of \(c(X)\) is defined to be the number of chords crossing \(c(X)\) from left to right minus the number crossing from right to left. If this index is divisible by 4 then we call its parity even, otherwise its parity is odd. Again, all classical diagrams have even crossings. The author also considers free diagrams in which there is not only no distinction between over and undercrossings (flat ones) but the local orientation at each crossing is indistinct. He gives examples of non trivial free knots which contradicts a conjecture of Turaev. The main theorem used is:

An odd irreducible diagram \(K\) is minimal, that is, for every diagram \(K'\) representing the same free knot, the diagram \(K'\) has more crossings than \(K\).

Other results and definitions are given in this long but interesting paper. There are too many to discuss in this review.

editorial_contributions.text:
The main objects in the present paper are virtual links and their virtual quandles. Virtual knots and links were introduced by \textit{L. H. Kauffman} [Eur. J. Comb. 20, No. 7, 663--690 (1999; Zbl 0938.57006)]. The virtual quandle was introduced by the present author [Acta Appl. Math. 72, No. 3, 295--309 (2002; Zbl 1003.57005)] as a virtual version of the knot quandle proposed independently by \textit{D. Joyce} [J. Pure Appl. Algebra 23, 37--65 (1982; Zbl 0474.57003)] and \textit{S. V. Matveev} [Math. USSR, Sb. 47, 73--83 (1984; Zbl 0523.57006)]. In fact, it is a quandle \((M, \circ)\) with a unary operation \(f\) such that: (1) \(f\) is invertible, (2) \(\circ\) is idempotent, (3) \(\circ\) is left invertible, (4) \(f\) is a quandle automorphism. Note that a quandle is an object satisfying the conditions (2) and (3) above. Namely, the operation \(f\) in a virtual quandle is added for virtual crossings.

Any group \(G\) can be transformed into a virtual quandle as in the case of ordinary quandles, for example, put \(a \circ b = b^{n} a b^{-n}\) for \(a\), \(b \in G\) and \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\) and let \(f\) be any automorphism of \(G\), or set \(a \circ b = ba^{-1}b\) for \(a\), \(b \in G\) and let \(f\) be any (anti-)automorphism of \(G\).

Given a virtual link diagram \(L\), we can construct its virtual quandle \(\mathcal{Q}(L)\) in any group \(G\). The virtual quandle \(\mathcal Q(L)\) is a virtual link invariant. (Please refer to the author's paper quoted above for details).

In the present paper, the author studies how to construct virtual link invariants with valuee in (infinite-dimensional) Lie algebras via virtual quandles in a Lie group. Given a virtual quandle in a Lie group \(G\), we can construct an algebra in its Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{g}\) by using a correspondence between \(G\) and \(\mathfrak{g}\) under the exponential map exp: \(\mathfrak{g} \rightarrow G\) with its inverse, the logarithm, log: \(G \rightarrow \mathfrak{g}\). Let \(K\) be a virtual link diagram. Then the author shows that the algebras in \(\mathfrak{g}\) associated with a virtual quandle \(\mathcal{Q}(K)\) in \(G\) are invariants of oriented virtual links, which are closely related to colorings of a virtual link diagram like quandles.

In the final section, the author explains how to work with the invariants.

editorial_contributions.text:
The paper under review considers the weight system of chord diagrams and Chinese character diagrams (which appear in the theory of Vassiliev invariants of knots) associated to the adjoint representation of the Lie algebra \(sl_n\). It is known by \textit{D. Bar-Natan} [Combinatorica 17, No. 1, 43-52 (1997; Zbl 0880.17005)] that the value \(W_{sl_n}(D)\) of each Chinese character diagram \(D\) with \(2l\) vertices evaluated by the weight system \(W_{sl_n}\) associated to the adjoint representation of \(sl_n\) is a polynomial in \(n\) of degree at most \(l+2\). The author generalizes this to the case of Chinese character diagrams possibly with univalent vertices. A similar result for the \(so_n\) case is also shown. 


Furthermore, it is shown that the degree \(l+2\) coefficient of \(W_{sl_n}(C)\) for a chord diagram \(C\) with \(l\) chords is the number of dividing the set of chords of \(C\) into the disjoint union of two subsets each with pairwise nonintersecting chords. However, it seems that this result follows almost directly from the above-mentioned paper, Proposition 1.2.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0997.00019].

editorial_contributions.text: Virtual knot theory is a generalization of classical knot theory. Virtual links have diagrams which contain in addition to the classical crossings (where one arc passes over another) virtual crossings, that is points of self-intersections of the arcs in the diagram. The equivalence of virtual knots and links is defined combinatorically by generalized Reidemeister moves involving also the virtual crossings. In this paper the author generalizes classical link invariants (such as the knot quandle, the knot fundamental group, the Alexander module and coloring invariants) to virtual link invariants. His work generalizes a construction of a knot quandle for virtual knots by \textit{L. H. Kauffman} [Eur. J. Comb. 20, No. 7, 663-690 (1999; Zbl 0938.57006)] to a virtual quandle \(Q\). From \(Q\) a virtual Alexander module can be computed. That in turn leads to a definition of a virtual Alexander polynomial that has no analogue in the classical case (i.e. it vanishes on classical links).

editorial_contributions.text:
The knot theory multiverse contains various generalizations of knots in \(S^3\): virtual knots, flat knots, free knots, pseudoknots, knots in thickened surfaces, homotopy classes of Gauss words, etc. An important aspect of the theory of these generalizations is that they are related by so-called functorial maps. A functorial map is map from a knot theory \(\mathcal{K}\) to another knot theory \(\mathcal{K}'\) such that if two knots are Reidemeister equivalent in \(\mathcal{K}\), then their images are Reidemeister equivalent in \(\mathcal{K}'\). In each case, the notion of Reidemeister equivalence is local to the particular generalized knot theory. An example of a functorial map is the inclusion of the classical knots into the virtual knots.
ewline In the reviewed paper, the author proves the surprising result that there is a non-trivial functorial mapping from virtual knots to classical knots. Given a virtual knot diagram \(K\), it is shown that there is a classical knot \(\overline{K}\) which can be obtained from \(K\) by deleting some of its crossings (i.e. making them virtual). Moreover, \(\overline{K}=K\) if and only if \(K\) is a classical. The map (or projection) is functorial in the sense that if \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are equivalent virtual knots, then \(\overline{K}_1\) and \(\overline{K}_2\) are equivalent classical knots. The projection is also surjective: every classical knot is in the image of the projection. 
ewline There is a very interesting corollary to this result. Suppose that you have a classical knot \(K\). If we consider \(K\) as a virtual knot, then \(K\) will have diagrams which have both classical and virtual crossings. Among all such diagrams, there is a smallest number \(\mu_{	ext{virtual}}\) of classical crossings. On the other hand, if we consider only classical diagrams to which \(K\) is equivalent, then we also have a minimal number of classical crossings, \(\mu_{	ext{classical}}\). Must it be the case that \(\mu_{	ext{classical}}=\mu_{	ext{virtual}}\)? The existence of the projection conclusively proves that \(\mu_{	ext{classical}}=\mu_{	ext{virtual}}\). A similar corollary about the bridge number of a classical knot is also established. 
ewline 
ewline The author also shows that the projection can be established in at least two distinct ways. Both methods rely on the following lemma/theorem: if the underlying surface of a virtual knot diagram \(K\) is not of minimal genus, then there is a knot diagram \(K' \leftrightharpoons K\) that can be obtained from \(K\) by deleting some of its crossings. Then beginning with a virtual knot diagram, the projection deletes classical crossings until a knot diagram is obtained such that its underlying surface is of minimal genus. The map may then be completed either by applying a projection due to I. Nikonov (a full proof is provided) or by using a projection derived from parity groups. The parity group method turns out to be the more discriminating of the two methods.
ewline The author notes that it would be preferable for the projection to be computed directly from a Gauss diagram of the virtual knot. Indeed, both current methods require a reduction to a diagram whose underlying surface realizes the minimal genus. The author also asks whether there is a projection map satisfying the same properties as the given maps but which preserves as many classical crossings as possible.

title.title: Knot theory

editorial_contributions.text: In previous papers, the author constructed the Khovanov theory for virtual knots, but the Khovanov complex was well defined for all virtual links only over \(\mathbb{Z}_2\), and the Khovanov homology with arbitrary coefficients was defined only for virtual knots corresponding to orientable atoms. In the present paper, the Khovanov complex with arbitrary coefficients for arbitrary virtual knots is constructed. Key ideas to overcome the difficulty are the change of basis of the Frobenius algebra representing the Khovanov homology of the unknot and the exterior product instead of the usual tensor product for the spaces corresponding to the circles. The method above works for twisted virtual knots in the sense of Bourgoin and Viro.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The present paper gives a quick survey of virtual and classical knot theory and presents a list of unsolved problems about virtual knots and links. These are all problems in low-dimensional topology with a special emphasis on virtual knots. In particular, we touch new approaches to knot invariants such as biquandles and Khovanov homology theory. Connections to other geometrical and combinatorial aspects are also discussed.

editorial_contributions.text:
For an oriented long free knot \(K\), the author defines an invariant \(l(K)\) and \(L(K)=|l(K)|\) by using \textit{refined parities} due to himself [Sb. Math. 201, No. 5, 693--733 (2010; Zbl 1210.57010)]. Then \(l(K)\) detects non-invertibility as a long free knot (Corollary 2), and \(L(K)\) is an invariant as an oriented/unoriented free knot (Corollary 3). An example is raised which shows \(L(K)\) is a non-trivial invariant (Figure 7). The main theorem of the present paper is that \(L(K)\) is a cobordism invariant, and \(L(K)\neq 0\) implies \(K\) is not null-cobordant (\(=\) is non-trivial) (Theorem 4 in Section 6).

A \textit{free knot} and a \textit{free link} are the same notion as a \textit{Gauss word} and a \textit{Gauss phrase} respectively in nanoword theory due to \textit{V.~Turaev} (for example, see [Int. Math. Res. Not. 2006, No. 25, Article ID 84098, 23 p. (2006; Zbl 1118.57009)]), which forget information of the local intersection number at every crossing from a flat virtual knot and a flat virtual link. A free knot is also regarded as a chord diagram and a framed \(4\)-valent graph. Here the meaning of `framed' is that every \(4\)-valent vertex is rigid as an intersection of two local arcs but the sign (the local intersection number) is not determined even if it is oriented and base-pointed. The author uses them effectively. A chord diagram is used when equivalence relations induced from Reidemeister moves are defined (Subsection 1.2), and when notions of the \textit{gaussian parity} and the \textit{refined gaussian parity} of every crossing is introduced (Definition 4 in Subsection 1.3). A framed \(4\)-valent graph is used when a notion of \textit{cobordism} is introduced (Section 4).

In Definition 2 and 3 in Subsection 1.3, notions of the gaussian parity and the refined gaussian parity for a free knot are generalized as a \textit{parity} and a \textit{refined parity}, respectively. A parity \(p(v)\) of a crossing \(v\) is valued in \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}=\{0, 1\}\): \(v\) is \textit{even} if \(p(v)=0\), and \(v\) is \textit{odd} if \(p(v)=1\). A refined parity divides the odd crossings into two types: \textit{odd of the first type} and \textit{odd of the second type}. The generalized notions are defined relatively and axiomatically. In Section 3, it is pointed out that a parity is equivalent to an element with a certain restriction of the first cohomology class over \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\) for the free knot as a \(4\)-valent graph. In Section 2, an invariant of a free knot is defined, which is valued in a group \(G\) generated by \(a, b\) and \(b'\) with certain relations. By corresponding the crossings to \(a, b\) and \(b'\) (an even crossing to \(a\), an odd crossing of the first type to \(b\), and an odd crossing of the second type to \(b'\)), a free knot \(K\) determines the conjugacy class of an element in \(G\) of the form \((bb')^{4m}\)\ \((m\in \mathbb{Z})\). Then \(l(K)=4m\) and \(L(K)=4|m|\). In Section 4, a notion of \textit{cobordism} is introduced. Two free knots \(K\) and \(K'\) are \textit{cobordant} if there exists a singular annulus \(F\) surrounded by \(K\cup (-K')\), where the singular set of \(F\) consists of cusps, double lines and triple points.

As an alternative proof of non-triviality of free knots (Gauss words), I strongly recommend \textit{A.~Gibson}'s paper [Math. Ann. 349, No. 4, 871--887 (2011; Zbl 1242.57013)]. The present paper is full of new original ideas. Since free knot theory should be the core part of nanoword theory, I feel a sequence of the author's works is very important.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: In previous papers (see e.g. [\textit{V. O. Manturov}, Sb. Math. 201, No. 5, 693--733 (2010; Zbl 1210.57010)]), the author realized the following principle for many knot theories: if a knot diagram is complicated enough then it reproduces itself, i.e. a subdiagram of any other diagram equivalent to it. This principle is realized by diagram-valued invariants \([\,\cdot\,]\) of knots such that \([K] = K\) for \(K\) complicated enough. It turns out that in the case of free braids, the same principle can be realized in an unexpectedly easy way by a one-term invariant formula.

title.title: One-term parity bracket for braids

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: In [\textit{V. O. Manturov}, ``On Free Knots'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:0901.2214}], the second named author constructed the bracket invariant \([\cdot]\) of virtual knots valued in \textit{pictures} (linear combinations of virtual knot diagrams with some crossing information omitted), such that for many diagrams \(K\), the following formula holds: \([K] = \widetilde{K}\), where \(\widetilde{K}\) is the underlying graph of the diagram, i.e. the value of the invariant on a diagram equals the diagram itself with some crossing information omitted. This phenomenon allows one to reduce many questions about virtual knots to questions about their diagrams. In [\textit{S. Nelson}, \textit{M. E. Orrison} and \textit{V. Rivera}, J. Knot Theory Ramifications 26, No. 5, Article ID 1750034, 24 p. (2017; Zbl 1396.57023)], the authors discovered the following phenomenon: having a biquandle coloring of a certain knot, one can enhance various state-sum invariants (say, Kauffman bracket) by using various coefficients depending on colors. Taking into account that the parity can be treated in terms of biquandles, we bring together the two ideas from these papers and construct the picture-valued parity-biquandle bracket for classical and virtual knots. This is an invariant of virtual knots valued in pictures. Both the parity bracket and Nelson-Orrison-Rivera invariants are partial cases of this invariant, hence this invariant enjoys many properties of various kinds. Recently, the authors together with E. Horvat and S. Kim have found that the picture-valued phenomenon works in the classical case.

editorial_contributions.text:
A knot \(J\) in \(S^3\) is fibered if the knot complement \(\overline{S^3-V(J)}\) fibers locally trivially over \(S^1\), where \(V(J)\) denotes a regular neighborhood of \(J\). Let \(J\) be a fibered knot in \(S^3\) with a given fibration \(p : \overline{S^3-V(J)} \to S^1\) and \(\Sigma=p^{-1}(z_0)\) for some \(z_0 \in S^1\). Let \(K\) be a knot in \(\overline{S^3-V(J)}\) such that \(\text{lk}(J,K)=0\). There is an orientation preserving homeomorphism from the infinite cyclic cover \(M_J\) of the complement of \(J\) to \(\Sigma\times (0,1)\). Let \(\pi_J : M_J \to \overline{S^3-V(J)}\) be the covering map. Let \(K'\) be a knot in \(M_J\) such that \(\pi_J(K')=K\). In this case, the lift \(K'\) of \(K\) can be considered as a knot in \(\Sigma\times [0,1]\) via the inclusion map \(\Sigma\times(0,1) \to \Sigma\times [0,1]\). Let \(\widehat{K}\) denote the virtual knot representing the stability class of \(K'\) in \(\Sigma\times [0,1]\).

In the paper under review, the authors call a virtual knot \(\widehat{K}\) obtained in this way a \textit{virtual cover} of \(K\) relative to the triple \((J, p, \Sigma)\). To describe virtual covers, the authors introduce the notion of a \textit{special Seifert form} of the link \(J \cup K\), which consists of a Seifert surface \(\Sigma\) of \(J\) and finitely many \(3\)-balls in \(S^3\) satisfying certain conditions with \(K\). When knots are given in a special Seifert form, virtual covers are essentially unique up to equivalence of virtual knots. It is proved that every virtual knot is a virtual cover of some knot and that if \(\widehat{K}_1\) and \(\widehat{K}_2\) are virtual covers of two knots \(K_1\) and \(K_2\), respectively, relative to \((J,p,\Sigma)\) and if there is a smooth ambient isotopy taking \(K_1\) to \(K_2\) with fixed \(V(J)\), then \(\widehat{K}_1\) and \(\widehat{K}_2\) are equivalent as virtual knots.

Also, the authors investigate what can be said about a classical knot from its virtual covers. For example, they prove that there is a pair of figure eight knots \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) in \(S^3\) and a trefoil knot \(T\) in \(\overline{S^3-(V(K_1)\cup V(K_2))}\) such that there is no ambient isotopy taking \(K_1\) to \(K_2\) fixing \(T\), and also prove a similar result for a knot \(K\) and its inverse \(K^{-1}\).

 These results are established by applying parity arguments to virtual covers and are used to present some applications to classical knots. Accordingly, virtual covers provide a way to study classical knots with the methods of virtual knot theory. This is distinct from the usual way in which virtual knots are studied with the methods of classical knot theory. Typically, classical knots are considered as a subset of the set of virtual knots. The alternative approach advocated in the present paper allows us to exploit both the non-trivial ambient topology and the intrinsic combinatorial properties of virtual knots.

title.title: Fibered knots and virtual knots

editorial_contributions.text:
One of the big problems in the theory of Khovanov homology [\textit{M. Khovanov}, Duke Math. J. 101, No.~3, 359--426 (2000; Zbl 0960.57005)] is how to extend it from a theory which works on knots and links in \(\mathbb R^3\), to a full TFT, also categorifying quantum invariants of 3-manifolds, and many partial answers are known. Since the complex from which Khovanov homology is computed has its chains generated from a bifurcation cube of ''splittings'' of a knot diagram, one step in this direction is to work with knots on higher genus surfaces, or even better with virtual knots. A \textsl{virtual knot} [\textit{L. H. Kauffman}, Eur. J. Comb. 20, No.7,663--690 (1999; Zbl 0938.57006)] is an equivalence class of planar diagrams called \textsl{virtual knot diagrams} (4-valent graphs in which only some of the vertices need be endowed with additional over/under crossing information, the others remaining as \textsl{virtual crossings}) under a set of generalized Reidemeister moves. The paper under review produces a slightly different chain complex and differentials to generate Khovanov homology for virtual knots over arbitrary coefficient systems, in a way consistent with, but extending previous models. In the past there have been similar attempts, but because of problems with signs, the theories worked only over \(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\). 

Suppose \(K\) is a virtual knot diagram. By a state is meant a choice of smoothing at each \textsl{classical} crossing in \(K\). Each state determines a splitting of \(K\), which will be a collection of circles (say \(k\)), to which is associated a vector space which is the exterior product (not tensor/symmetric product) of \(k\) copies of a 2-dimensional vector space \(V\), along with a chosen basis formed from bases \(\{1,\pm{}X\}\) (signs dependent on orientations) for the \(k\) factors. This generates a complex of chains, \([[K]]\), doubly graded by height (number of \(B\)-smoothings in the state) and grading (height plus difference in numbers of 1's and \(X\)'s in chain). States form a \textsl{bifurcation cube}, edges corresponding to changing the smoothing at one crossing between types \(A\) and \(B\). States joined by an edge have numbers of circles in their split diagrams, either identical or differing by one, as the affected circles may transform \(1\rightarrow1\), \(1\rightarrow2\) or \(2\rightarrow1\). A partial differential is defined corresponding to each classical crossing (the total differential being the sum of the partial differentials) by defining suitable maps \(\Delta:V\longrightarrow{}V\wedge{}V\), \(m:V\wedge{}V\longrightarrow{}V\) by \(\Delta(1)=1\wedge{}X_2+X_1\wedge1\), \(\Delta(X)=x_1\wedge{}X_2\), \(m(X_1\wedge{}X_2)=0\) while \(1\) behaves like a unit under the multiplication map \(m\). The main theorems are that the differential on the complex \({\mathcal C}(K)=[[K]]{n_+-2n_-}[-n_-]\) obtained from \([[K]]\) by shifting both the grading and height (where \(n_\pm\) denote the numbers of positively and negatively oriented crossings in \(K\)) defines a differential bigraded complex (that is \(\partial^2=0\)) whose homology groups are invariant under generalized Reidemeister moves and which, in the case that \(K\) is a virtual link diagram of an orientable atom, agree with the standard Khovanov homology. The methods of the paper can also be applied for `twisted virtual knots' and the paper concludes with some remarks about generalizations of various results known for Khovanov homology of classical knots/links to the virtual cases.

editorial_contributions.text: Consider a 4-regular graph \(G\) where each vertex \(v\) been given a pairing of its incident edges, say \(e_1\) with \(e_2\) and \(e_3\) with \(e_4\). When is there a planar embedding of \(G\) such that at each vertex \(e_1\) appears opposite \(e_2\) in the local rotation at \(v\)? Vassiliev conjectured that there is a planar embedding if and only if the graph contains no pair of (simple) cycles intersecting in a single vertex such that at that vertex \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) belong to the same cycle. In this paper the author proves Vassiliev's conjecture. One direction is easy: if there is a planar embedding, then there is no such pair of cycles. The other direction requires some care. The proof leads to a quadratic-time algorithm to determine if the desired embedding exists.

editorial_contributions.text:
The Khovanov complex of a knot or link diagram is a bigraded chain complex whose chain groups are generated by smoothed states of the diagram. The boundary map is a sum of linear maps for each pair of states which differ by a single smoothing, with maps where one component splits into two corresponding to comultiplication and maps where two components fuse into one corresponding to multiplication. Diagrams related by Reidemeister moves then yield chain-homotopic complexes, so the resulting homology groups form a knot invariant, with the Jones polynomial as the Euler characteristic.

When this procedure is applied to virtual knots and links, there is a problem -- not every map splits or fuses components; some maps preserve the number of components. The author of this paper extends the Khovanov complex to virtual knots by setting such maps to zero, resulting in a chain complex over \(\mathbb{Z}_2\). Generalizations involving Frobenius extensions are explored, and the author's notion of \textit{atoms} is discussed.

title.title: Maps to virtual braids and braid representations

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: This paper is the first one in the sequence of papers about a simple class of framed 4-graphs; the goal of this paper is to collect some well-known results on planarity and to reformulate them in the language of minors. The goal of the whole sequence is to prove analogs of the Robertson-Seymour-Thomas theorems for framed 4-graphs: namely, we shall prove that many minor-closed properties are classified by finitely many excluded graphs. From many points of view, framed 4-graphs are easier to consider than general graphs; on the other hand, framed 4-graphs are closely related to many problems in graph theory.

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: In Ref. 6, the author has constructed natural maps from fundamental groups of topological spaces (restricted configuration spaces) to the groups \(G_n^k\). In the present paper, we show that in the case of \(n = k+1\), the group \(G_{k + 1}^k\) is isomorphic to the fundamental group of some (quotient space of) some configuration space up to finite index subgroups. In particular, this leads to the solution of word and conjugacy problems in \(G_4^3\) and sheds light on \(G_{k + 1}^k\) for higher \(k\).

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1440.13001].

editorial_contributions.text:
In this paper, the author applies the concept parity to free knots and links and virtual knots and links. Parity is used to construct new invariants of free and virtual knots and used to prove theorems about minimality and non-triviality. Section 2 contains an overview of virtual knot theory which is followed by an introduction to free knots and links -- equivalence classes of framed 4-graphs modulo the virtual Reidemeister moves.

In Section 3, the author introduces the concept of parity and specifically defines Gaussian parity, in which each crossing in the diagram is designated as even or odd. The behavior of parity under the Reidemeister moves is discussed. A functorial map on the set of virtual knots is defined using parity. Under this map, crossings with odd parity are virtualized and the number of classical crossings in the image is less than or equal to the number of classical crossings in the pre-image. This functorial map gives rise to a parity hierachy and the applications of this are explored.

In Section 4, for a framed 4-graph \( \Gamma\), parity is used to define a cohomology class on elements of \( H_1 ( \Gamma, \mathbb{Z}_2 ) \). The elements of the homology class are generated by the halves of the graph obtained by smoothing a vertex. In Section 5, the author defines knot invariants using parity. The invariant \( [ \Gamma ] \) is obtained by summing over states with 1 component; the states are obtained by smoothing even crossings. The author also defines an even Kauffman bracket. Applications of these invariants and references are provided in the article. The author also discusses results involving atoms and parity and an even analogue of Turaev's cobracket.

In the concluding section, the author constructs a group invariant using parity. The group \(G\) is \( \{ a,b,b' | a{}^2 =b{}^2 = b'{}^2 =1, ab = b' a \} \). From a Gauss diagram \(D\) of a knot, a word \( \gamma (D) \) is constructed based on the parity of the crossings. As an element of \(G\), \( \gamma(D) \) is an invariant of free knots. The author concludes with an example of a free knot that is shown to be non-trivial using parity.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1237.57001].

title.title: The Khovanov complex and minimal knot diagrams

editorial_contributions.text:
In this paper, the authors introduce the notion of a parity for 2-knots/links as an analog to a parity for 1-dimensional (virtual) knots. The authors define the Gaussian parity for abstract and free 2-knots, by defining that of a double line of a spherical diagram, and then generalize it to the notion of a parity. A parity is a mapping from the set of double lines of 2-link spherical diagrams to \(\mathbb{Z}_2\), satisfying certain axioms (I)--(IV). In particular, the Gaussian parity is a parity. Further, the authors introduce the notion of a weak parity. The notion of a parity refines invariants of 2-knots/links: the parity of the number of triple points of a diagram is an invariant of (free) 2-knots, and a parity quandle is an invariant of abstract 2-links. The paper is closed by giving a list of open problems.

We review the main terms. A 2-knot (respectively 2-link) is a smooth embedding of a 2-sphere (respectively disjoint union of 2-spheres) into \(\mathbb{R}^4\) or \(S^4\) up to isotopy. A spherical diagram is a 2-complex consisting of a sphere, a set of disjoint disks on it, and a set of marked curves on it, satisfying certain conditions. In particular, from a 2-knot/link, we derive its spherical diagram. An abstract 2-knot is an equivalence class of spherical diagrams modulo moves corresponding to Roseman moves. A free 2-knot is an abstract 2-knot without over/under information for double and triple points.

title.title: Parities on 2-knots and 2-links

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Recently, the author discovered an interesting class of knot-like objects called free knots. These purely combinatorial objects are equivalence classes of Gauss diagrams modulo Reidemeister moves (the same notion in the language of words was introduced by \textit{V. Turaev} [Proc. Lond. Math. Soc. (3) 95, No. 2, 360--412 (2007; Zbl 1145.57018)], who thought all free knots to be trivial). As it turned out, these new objects are highly nontrivial, and even admit nontrivial cobordism classes. An important issue is the existence of invariants where a diagram evaluates to itself which makes such objects ``similar'' to free groups: An element has its minimal representative which ``lives inside'' any representative equivalent to it. In this paper, we consider generalizations of free knots by means of (finitely presented) groups. These new objects have lots of nontrivial properties coming from both knot theory and group theory. This connection allows one not only to apply group theory to various problems in knot theory but also to apply Reidemeister moves to the study of (finitely presented) groups. Groups appear naturally in this setting when graphs are embedded in surfaces.

title.title: Reidemeister moves and groups

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: On the basis of the notion of parity introduced recently by the author, for each positive integer \( m\) we construct invariants of long virtual knots with values in some simply defined group \( \mathcal {G}_m\); conjugacy classes of this group play a role as invariants of compact virtual knots. By construction, each of the invariants is unaltered by the move of \(virtualization\). Factorization of the group algebra of the corresponding group leads to invariants of finite order of (long) virtual knots that do not change under virtualization.

The central notion used in the construction of the invariants is \(parity\): the crossings of diagrams of free knots are endowed with an additional structure -- each crossing is declared to be even or odd, where even crossings behave regularly under Reidemeister moves.

title.title: Parity, free knots, groups, and invariants of finite type

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper presents various results concerning virtual knots, virtual links and long virtual knots.

Section~3 of the paper deals with the problem of algorithmically recognizing virtual links.

There are algorithms to determine whether two classical knots are equivalent or not. For example, Haken and Hemion's algorithm [\textit{G. Hemion}, The classification of knots and 3-dimensional spaces. Oxford Science Publications. Oxford: Oxford University Press. (1992; Zbl 0771.57001)] or the algorithm given in [\textit{J. Hass}, Chaos Solitons Fractals 9, No.~4--5, 569--581 (1998; Zbl 0935.57014)]. In the paper under review, an algorithm is described for determining whether two virtual links are equivalent or not. This algorithm is based on Haken's theory for the algorithmic recognizability of Haken manifolds and a result of Kuperberg (any virtual link can be uniquely represented as a link in a thickened oriented surface) [\textit{G. Kuperberg}, Algebr. Geom. Topol. 3, 587--591 (2003; Zbl 1031.57010)].

Section~4 of the paper is concerned with behaviour of the underlying genus of a virtual knot under composition. 

The composite of two virtual knots is formed in the same way as the composite of two classical knots. However, it is well known that, unlike classical knots, the composite of a pair of virtual knots is not well-defined. Picking different ways to form the composite of a pair of virtual knots may result in different virtual knots. For two virtual knots \(K_1\) and \(K_2\), let \(K_1 \sharp K_2\) denote any composite of \(K_1\) and \(K_2\).

For a virtual knot \(K\), the underlying genus of \(K\) is the minimal genus over all surfaces on which a diagram of \(K\) can be drawn without requiring virtual crossings. This is also known as the supporting genus of \(K\) (for example, [\textit{N. Kamada}, Algebr. Geom. Topol. 4, 1083--1101 (2004; Zbl 1066.57018)]). Let \(g(K)\) denote the underlying genus of \(K\). It is proven in the paper that for any virtual knots \(K_1\) and \(K_2\), \(g(K_1 \sharp K_2)\) is greater than or equal to \(g(K_1) + g(K_2) - 1\). Furthermore, if \(g(K_1)\) or \(g(K_2)\) is zero, then \(g(K_1 \sharp K_2)\) is greater than or equal to \(g(K_1) + g(K_2)\). These inequalities are then used to show that if \(K_1 \sharp K_2\) is the trivial knot, then both \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) must be trivial. 

Section~5 of the paper gives, in more detail, results that previously appeared in the paper [\textit{V. O. Manturov}, Dokl. Math. 71, No. 2, 253--255 (2005); translation from Dokl. Akad. Nauk, Ross. Akad. Nauk 401, No. 5, 595--598 (2005; Zbl 1272.57005)].

A long virtual knot (also known as an open virtual knot) is a virtual tangle with a single open component. The closure of a long virtual knot, which is the operation which joins the two ends of the tangle together, results in a virtual knot. For two oriented long virtual knots \(K_1\) and \(K_2\), the concatenation of \(K_1\) and \(K_2\), written \(K_1 \sharp K_2\), is the oriented long virtual knot given by joining the end of \(K_1\) to the beginning of \(K_2\). This operation is well-defined and under it the set of oriented long virtual knots becomes a semigroup.

An algebraic object called a long groupoid is defined in the paper. The paper shows how to associate a long groupoid to an oriented long virtual knot \(K\) and proves that it is an invariant of \(K\). This invariant is a generalization of the virtual quandle invariant of virtual knots [\textit{V. O. Manturov}, Acta Appl. Math. 72, No.~3, 295--309 (2002; Zbl 1003.57005)]. The definition of the long groupoid invariant is also given in the paper [\textit{V. O. Manturov}, J. Knot Theory Ramification 13, No.~8, 1029--1039 (2004; Zbl 1064.57005)] (in that paper a long groupoid is called a long quandle).

The long groupoid invariant is used to show that there exist oriented long virtual knots \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) such that \(K_1 \sharp K_2\) is not equivalent to \(K_2 \sharp K_1\). In other words, in general, long virtual knots do not commute. An example is also given where the invariant can be used to distinguish a pair of oriented long virtual knots for which the closure, in each case, gives the trivial knot.

editorial_contributions.text:
The present author introduced parity theory in [Sb. Math. 201, No. 5, 693--733 (2010; Zbl 1210.57010)]. As an application to virtual knot theory he gave parity conditions for virtual knots and for free knots and showed for example that there are infinitely many inequivalent free knots, thus answering a problem of \textit{V. Turaev}, who conjectured that all free knots are trivial [Proc. Lond. Math. Soc. (3) 95, No. 2, 360--412 (2007; Zbl 1145.57018)].

In the article under review, the author develops further this parity theory. He constructs new parities for two-component virtual and free links. He also uses the parity bracket and Turaev cobracket to construct invariants of free links and gives an illustration with some examples. One can use the new parities in many problems where parities were already previously applied.

editorial_contributions.text:
A four-valent framed graph is a 4-regular graph with opposite edge structure at vertices specified. The author discusses the problem of detecting the least (highest) genus of a surface where a given four-valent framed graph can be embedded. The aim of the paper is to connect the problem above to several problems which arise in knot theory and combinatorics: Vassiliev invariants and weight systems coming from Lie algebras, Boolean matrices etc., and to give both partial solutions to the problem above and new formulations of it in the language of knot theory.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1205.57002].

editorial_contributions.text:
In virtual knot theory, there are three kinds of crossing numbers. For a given virtual knot diagram \(D\), we can consider the number of classical crossings, the number of virtual crossings and the sum of them. Usually we call them the classical crossing number, the virtual crossing number and the crossing number of \(D\). For a virtual knot \(K\), the minimum of these taken over all diagrams of \(K\) are called the classical crossing number of \(K\), the virtual crossing number of \(K\) and the crossing number of \(K\), respectively. It is an important problem to find out some relations between these crossing numbers or to give some lower bounds for them from virtual knot invariants.

For example a natural question is: can we find a virtual knot which satisfies that the virtual crossing number is greater than or equal to the classical crossing number? In the paper under review, the author proves that there exists a family of virtual knots \(K_i\) such that when \(i\) tends to infinity the virtual crossing numbers grows quadratically with respect to the classical crossing numbers. As a corollary this gives an affirmative answer to the question above. The construction of \(K_i\) mainly follows from the fact that there is a family of trivalent graphs for which the crossing number grows quadratically with respect to the number of vertices.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We construct a picture-valued invariant of classical knots by using the group $G_n^3$ and the plat closure of braids. We introduce a modification of the group $G_n^3$ and define a map from the braid group to framed 6-valent graphs with leaves. Each 6-valent vertex corresponds to the moment when three points become collinear. By using this construction, we obtain a knot invariant valued in equivalence classes of graphs modulo local moves. Our invariant provides a new graphical approach to the study of classical knots.

title.title: Recognition of virtual braids.

editorial_contributions.text: According to Alexander's theorem, every link admits a representation by a closed braid. Markov proved that two braids \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) represent the same link if and only if \(\alpha\) can be transformed to \(\beta\) by using a sequence of local transformations called Markov moves. In the present paper, the author introduces the notion of quasitoric braids and shows that all link isotopy classes can be encoded by quasitoric braids. It is worth mentioning that quasitoric braids represent a very small class of braids that forms a subgroup of the braid group. This subgroup contains the pure braids.

title.title: Labels instead of coefficients: a label bracket which dominates the Jones polynomial, the Kuperberg bracket, and the normalised arrow polynomial

editorial_contributions.text:
Virtual knots are defined as virtual knot diagrams modulo generalized Reidemeister moves. Other local moves can be defined on virtual knot diagrams. A crossing change is a move where the over and under strands at a real crossing are swapped. A virtual switch (also known as a virtualization) takes a real crossing and adds one virtual crossing above it and one virtual crossing below it (this move is shown, for example, in [\textit{L. H. Kauffman}, Atti Semin. Mat. Fis. Univ. Modena 49, Suppl., 241--282 (2001; Zbl 1072.57004)]). Free knots are virtual knots modulo crossing changes and virtual switches. Equivalently, free knots can be defined (as they are in this paper) as chord diagrams modulo certain relations corresponding to Reidemeister moves. 

Free knots were first defined by Turaev in [\textit{V. Turaev}, Proc. Lond. Math. Soc. (3) 95, No. 2, 360--412 (2007; Zbl 1145.57018)] as a particular example of nanowords. The name ``free knots'' was given to these objects by \textit{V. O. Manturov}, [''On free knots.'' arXiv:math.GT/0901.2214]. They are also known as homotopy classes of Gauss words [\textit{A. Gibson}, ''Homotopy invariants of Gauss words.'' arXiv:math.GT/0902.0062]. Turaev conjectured that these objects are trivial, in other words all free knots are equivalent to the unknot [\textit{V. Turaev}, Jpn. J. Math. (3) 2, No.~1, 1--39 (2007; Zbl 1162.68034)]. However, it was shown independently by\textit{V. O. Manturov} [op. cit.] and the reviewer [op. cit.] that non-trivial free knots exist. In fact, in both papers it was shown that there are infinitely many different free knots. 

From the definition of free knots it is clear that each virtual knot has an underlying free knot which is invariant under the generalized Reidemeister moves. Non-triviality of the underlying free knot implies non-triviality of the virtual knot itself. It should be noted that for any free knot \(K\) there are infinitely many virtual knots for which the underlying free knot is \(K\). For example, the free knot underlying any classical knot is the trivial free knot. 

In this paper, a new sequence of invariants is constructed for free knots. For each positive integer \(m\), the authors define a group \(G_m\) (in the paper the subscript is omitted). The group \(G_1\) is isomorphic to the infinite dihedral group. The authors then give a method to assign a conjugacy class of \(G_m\) to any chord diagram. This conjugacy class is an invariant of the free knot the chord diagram represents. An example of a non-trivial free knot detectable by this invariant in the case where \(m\) is equal to \(1\) is given in the paper.

title.title: Knots and the bracket calculus

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: The main goal of the present paper is to construct new invariants of knots with additional structure by adding new gradings to the Khovanov complex. The ideas given below work in the case of virtual knots, closed braids and some other cases of knots with additional structure. The source of our additional grading may be topological or combinatorial; it is axiomatised for many partial cases. As a byproduct, this leads to a complex which in some cases coincides (up to grading renormalisation) with the usual Khovanov complex and in some other cases with the Lee-Rasmussen complex.
The grading we are going to construct behaves well with respect to some generalisations of the Khovanov homology, e.g., Frobenius extensions. These new homology theories give sharper estimates for some knot characteristics, such as minimal crossing number, atom genus, slice genus, etc.
Our gradings generate a natural filtration on the usual Khovanov complex. There exists a spectral sequence starting with our homology and converging to the usual Khovanov homology.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1154.82001].

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The \(VA\)-polynomial proposed in the author's earlier paper [Acta Appl. Math. 72, No.~3, 295--309 (2002; Zbl 1003.57005)] for virtual knots and links is considered in this paper. One goal here is to refine the definition of this polynomial to the case of the ring \(\mathbb Z\) in place of the field \(\mathbb Q\). Moreover, the approach in the paper mentioned makes it possible to recognize ``long virtual knots'' obtained from equivalent virtual knots by cutting at various points. An invariant of long virtual knots that is based on the same technique as the \(VA\)-polynomial is proposed. Some properties of the \(VA\)-polynomial are established. Furthermore, new invariants of virtual links and long virtual knots are constructed.

title.title: On polynomial invariants of virtual links

editorial_contributions.text:
The theory of virtual knots and related objects has expanded hugely since the first paper on the topic in 1999. This is, as far as I am aware, the first book on this topic and fulfills a definite need.

After a moving tribute to the first named author's father, Oleg Vassilievich Manturov, there are prefaces by Louis Kauffman and the authors.

The first chapter deals with the basic definitions and notions of classical and virtual knots. They show how a virtual knot can be represented by a knot in a thickened surface thus aligning a purely combinatorial notion with a topological object. The authors note that virtual knots map to welded knots by the ``forbidden move'' but omit in the text the reference [8] which is in the bibliography. One curiosity of virtual knots which does not happen with classical knots is the possibility of an odd crossing. That is travelling along the knot between the two occurences of a crossing there may be an odd number of other crossings.

In Chapter 2 the connection between virtual knots and three-dimensional topology, mentioned in the first chapter is amplified. A virtual knot can be represented by a knot in a thickened surface, that is a surface cross a unit interval and two such represent the same knot if they are equivalent under the equivalence generated by a homeomorphism of the ambient space taking one to the other and surgery of the three manifold avoiding the knot. So a virtual knot has a genus, being the minimum genus of the associated surface. The genus is zero if and only if the knot is classical. The important result here is the Kuperberg theorem which says that in the minimal surface situation virtual knot theory is the same as standard knot theory. So for example if a classical knot could be transformed to another by the equivalence described above then they would already be the same.

The authors then describe subadditive formulae for two types of connected sums. This involves the notion of a so-called ``singular knot'' being a representative of minimal genus which intersects the belt annulus of the thickened surface transversely in exactly one point. This name is doubly unfortunate, firstly because there is nothing singular in the usual sense and secondly and most importantly there is already a settled definition of a singular knot as a kind of generalised immersed knot.

In the final part of this chapter the authors describe a virtual version of Haken's algorithmic discrimination of two knots. It is a shame that the authors do not give more details and rely heavily on various references. Here is a verbatim quote from page 50. ``We are not going to give an accurate definition of a normal surface and a fundamental surface.'' If that is the case why bother to mention them? This kind of elision of details may be satisfactory for a research paper but not in a book where these fine points should be considered.

The title of Chapter 3 is ``Quandles (Distributive Groupoids) in Virtual Knot Theory''. It is most important that these concepts are considered in book form as they are now entering the mainstream of modern knot theory. Quandles and racks are a generalisation of groups but their binary operation is non associative and mirrors the group conjugacy operation. Quandles have a geometric description and an algebraic description, unlike biquandles which up to now have no geometric description. Quandles have ancestors such as the coloring invariant, the Alexander virtual module, flat virtual knots, Lie algebras etc. They can be applied to classical knots, virtual knots, long or otherwise, and hierarchies of virtual knots. This is all explained in Chapter 3.

In Chapter 4 the authors consider the Jones Polynomial. This invariant of knots is defined from the Kauffman bracket which leads to various generalisations such as the polynomial \(\Xi\) which is a stronger invariant for virtual knots than the Jones polynomial. Along the way they consider an ``atom''. This is a cell decomposition of a surface such that each vertex has degree 4, (so the 1-skeleton is the image of a number of immersed curves in general position). Moreover the 2-cells can be black and white coloured chess board fashion. For example a cell decomposition of the torus can be defined with 1-skeleton a meridian and longitude. However this is not an atom as it only has one 2-cell. If we now double the meridian and longitude then an atom results. But trebling fails, as can easily be seen.

Khovanov homology with \(\mathbb Z_2\)-coefficients is the topic of Chapter 5. The invention of the Khovanov complex was an important generalisation of the Jones polynomial for classical knots. Here, the authors explain how this construction can be generalised to virtual knots albeit with \(\mathbb Z_2\)-coefficients. The construction uses atoms as described in the previous chapter.

In Chapter 6 virtual braids are considered. As in the classical case virtual braids have a closure which is a virtual knot. There is also a corresponding Markov theorem and analogous Markov moves to which must be added some extra moves just for the virtual theory. The reviewer would have liked to see a better definition of these as a neophyte would find the construction by diagram here very confusing. The extension of the Burau representation and the Kauffman bracket polynomial for braids is given. An invariant of virtual braids, generalising the Artin representation into the automorphism group of a free group is given and its completeness for the case of two-strand virtual braids is shown.

The authors consider Vassiliev's invariants in Chapter 7. There is a reasonably coherent theory of ``classical'' knots with possible self intersections which make up the theory of Vassiliev's invariants. However, this is not yet remotely true for any Vassiliev type theory of virtual knots and this densely argued chapter reflects this. A list of subsections of this chapter gives some idea of its complexity: Framed Graphs, The Vassiliev invariants of classical knots and J-invariants of curves, The Goussarov-Polyak-Viro approach, The Kauffman approach, Invariants generated by the polynomial \(\Xi\), Vassiliev's invariants coming from the invariant \(\Xi\), Infinity of the number of long virtual knots, Graphs, chord diagrams and the Kauffman polynomial, Euler tours, Gauss circuits and rotating circuits, 4-Graphs and Euler tours, Framed 4-valent graphs and Euler tours, The existence of a Gauss circuit, The Gauss circuit, Adjacency matrices, A proof of Vassiliev's conjecture, Embeddings of framed 4-graphs.

Parity in knot theory is a speciality of the first named author and this is the topic of Chapter 8. The parity of a chord in a chord diagram can be defined to be the parity of the number of chords it crosses. It was Gauss who noted that the chord diagram obtained from an immersion of a circle in the plane always has chords with even parity. It follows that a chord diagram with one or more chords having odd parity can only be realised by a virtual knot. The theory of parities and how they relate to the Reidemeister moves is developed here as is the notion of free knots and various Lie type algebraic invariants.

The intersection graph of a chord diagram has one vertex for each chord and two vertices are joined by an edge if the coresponding chords cross. Two distinct chord diagrams may have the same intersection graph and some graphs may not be realisable as the intersection graph of a chord diagram. Nevertheless, useful invariants may be obtained from this concept. For example, the parity of a chord in a chord diagram is the parity of the valency of the corresponding vertex of the intersection graph. Such notions form the content of Chapter 9, the final chapter.

So in conclusion what can we say about this book? Firstly, the English is not too bad considering this is not the authors' native tongue. There is the usual problem with the definite and indefinite article experienced by speakers East of the Urals. Since I do not know the rules myself for their inclusion or otherwise how can non-native speakers be expected to know? The book is far too stuffed with material, some of which is covered too quickly and not in depth. A more measured approach would have produced 2 or possible 3 volumes. The index is too skimpy for a 521p book. For example, source, sink, source-sink condition and weld do not appear. Nevertheless despite these negative comments the authors are to be congratulated on producing a book covering material which has not appeared in book form before and hopefully later editions will eliminate the above concerns.

Preprint \url{arXiv:1501.05208}] the first author gave the definition of \(k\)-free braid groups \(G_n^k\). editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We construct graph-valued analogues of the Kuperberg sl(3) and \(G_2\) invariants for virtual knots. The restriction of the sl(3) and \(G_2\) invariants for classical knots coincides with the usual Homflypt sl(3) invariant and \(G_2\) invariants. For virtual knots and graphs these invariants provide new graphical information that allows one to prove minimality theorems and to construct new invariants for free knots (unoriented and unlabeled Gauss codes taken up to abstract Reidemeister moves). A novel feature of this approach is that some knots are of sufficient complexity that they evaluate themselves in the sense that the invariant is the knot itself seen as a combinatorial structure. The paper generalizes these structures to virtual braids and discusses the relationship with the original Penrose bracket for graph colorings.

editorial_contributions.text: This paper contains two representations of \(n\)-braids. One is geometric using \(n\) simple arcs joining \(n\) pairs of points on a plane. The other is algebraic using \(n\) words on \(n\) alphabets that can be read from the simple arcs. The latter representation dates back to the representation into the automorphism group of the free group by E. Artin. With these, the authors construct a simple complete combinatorial invariant for braids. This admits some generalizations, e.g., a complete invariant of spherical and cylindrical braids. The values of the invariant provide the complete algorithmic classification of the elements in the named braid group.

title.title: Group G_{n}^{3} and imaginary generators

editorial_contributions.text:
Virtual knot theory was introduced by \textit{L. H. Kauffman} [Eur. J. Comb. 20, No. 7, 663--690 (1999; Zbl 0938.57006)] as a generalization of classical knot theory. A virtual knot is an equivalence class of virtual knot diagrams modulo generalized Reidemeister moves. The notion of free link is a generalized notion of virtual link, in the sense that two representatives of free links represent the same equivalence class if and only if the corresponding virtual link diagrams are the same modulo some transformations (see [\textit{V. O. Manturov}, Sb. Math. 201, No. 5, 693--733 (2010; Zbl 1210.57010)] for more details).

In classical knot theory, knots and links can be represented as equivalence classes of braids modulo Markov moves. The authors of the paper under review investigate this situation in the context of free links. The authors define the group of free braids, prove the analogue of the Alexander theorem, that all free links can be obtained as closures of free braids and prove a Markov theorem, which gives necessary and sufficient conditions for two free braids to have the same free link closure

editorial_contributions.text:
For a given \(d\)-manifold \(M^d\) the authors consider the \((dn)\)-manifold \(M^{dn}\) of all \(n\)-vertex triangulations of \(M^d\) in three different ways: geometrical, topological and combinatorial. The manifold \(M^{dn}\) is possibly disconnected, each component defines an \(n\)-strand braid group as the fundamental group of that component.

As the main part of the paper the authors construct a mapping from such a braid group to the group \(\Gamma^{d+2}_n\). The groups \(\Gamma^k_n\) are defined in terms of bistellar flips (or Pachner moves) of \((k-2)\)-dimensional manifolds with \(n\) vertices. This construction allows to define topological or smooth invariants of the underlying manifold \(M^d\).

Additional remark: By considering these groups for all vertex links in a triangulated manifold, the work of A. Gaifullin shows that in the same spirit combinatorial calculations of characteristic classes are possible.

For an explicit example see \textit{D. Gorodkov} [Discrete Comput. Geom. 62, No. 2, 348--373 (2019; Zbl 1425.57016)].

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1470.65003].

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: This paper considers \(\ast\)-graphs in which all vertices have degree 4 or 6, and studies the question of calculating the genus of orientable 2-surfaces into which such graphs may be embedded. A \(\ast\)-graph is a graph endowed with a formal adjacency structure on the half-edges around each vertex, and an embedding of a \(\ast\)-graph is an embedding under which the formal adjacency relation on half-edges corresponds to the adjacency relation induced by the embedding. \(\ast\)-graphs are a natural generalization of four-valent framed graphs, which are four-valent graphs with an opposite half-edge structure.


 In [\textit{O. Manturov}, Dokl. Math. 79, No. 1, 56--58 (2009); translation from Dokl. Akad. Nauk, Ross. Akad. Nauk 424, No. 3, 308--310 (2009; Zbl 1309.05054)], the question of whether a four-valent framed graph admits a \(\mathbb Z_{2}\)-homologically trivial embedding into a given surface was shown to be equivalent to a problem on matrices. We show that a similar result holds for \(\ast\)-graphs in which all vertices have degree 4 or 6. This gives an algorithm in quadratic time to determine whether a \(\ast\)-graph admits an embedding into the plane.

editorial_contributions.text:
The main examples coming from \(G^k_n\)-theory are homomorphisms from the \(n\) strand pure braid group to the groups \(G^3_n\) and \(G^4_n\). If we consider the motion of \(n\) pairwise distinct points on the plane and choose the property ``some three points are collinear'', then we get a homomorphism from the pure \(n\) strand braid group \(PB_n\) to the group \(G^3_n\). If we choose the property ``some four points belong to the same circle or line'', we shall get a group homomorphism from \(PB_n\) to \(G^4_n\).

The groups \(G^k_n\) have connections to different algebraic structures, Coxeter groups, Kirillov-Fomin algebras, and cluster algebras. Study of the groups \(G^k_n\) led to, in particular, the construction of invariants, valued in free products of cyclic groups. All generators of the groups \(G^k_n\) are reflections which make them similar to Coxeter groups and not to braid groups. Nevertheless, there are many ways to enhance the groups \(G^k_n\) to get rid of this 2-torsion. Later the first and the fourth named author introduced and studied a second family of groups, denoted by \(\Gamma_n^k\), which are closely related to triangulations of manifolds.

The spaces of triangulations of a given manifold have been widely studied. The celebrated theorem of \textit{U. Pachner} [Eur. J. Comb. 12, No. 2, 129--145 (1991; Zbl 0729.52003)] says that any two triangulations of a given manifold can be connected by a sequence of bistellar moves or Pachner moves.

The group \(\Gamma_n^k\) naturally appears when considering the set of triangulations with a fixed number of points. There are two ways of introducing the groups \(\Gamma_n^k\): the geometrical one, which depends on the metric, and the topological one. The second one can be thought of as a ``braid group'' of the manifold and, by definition, is an invariant of the topological type of the manifold; in a similar way, one can construct the smooth version.

In Appendix A, the authors give a brief outline of free knot theory and parity theory, and then present an overview of some of the most recent developments of the theory. The authors concentrate on the notion of manifolds of triangulations, the construction of 3-free links arising from the groups \(G^k_n\), and the study of domino tilings of surfaces, which lead both to groups similar to \(\Gamma_n^4\), and to certain invariants of braids.

editorial_contributions.text:
The paper under review studies rhombille tilings of zonogons with \(2n\) vertices and the relations among flip operations, interpreted geometrically as stacking three-dimensional cubes. Two fundamental relations for flips are recalled, namely far-commutativity and the octagon relation, which originate from the cube recurrence.

The main results establish a precise correspondence between sequences of flips on rhombille tilings and elements of the group \(G^3_n\). This group is generated by involutions indexed by triples \(\{i,j,k\}\subset \{1,\dots,n \}\) and defined by commutativity relations together with a four-term relation corresponding to the octagon move; it was introduced earlier by the second author. For tilings of a zonogon in the plane, it is shown that all closed sequences of flips represent the trivial element of \(G^3_n\). In contrast, for rhombille tilings on non-orientable surfaces and in particular on the projective plane \(\mathbb{RP}^2\), the authors construct explicit closed sequences of flips whose images in \(G^3_n\) are nontrivial. Moreover, the paper relates flips to third Reidemeister moves via dual diagrams, thereby clarifying the appearance of the defining relations of \(G^3_n\).

title.title: The groups \(G_n^k\), \(2n\)-gon tilings, and stacking of cubes

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: The present paper is a review of the current state of Graph-Link Theory (graph-links are closely related to homotopy classes of looped interlacement graphs): a theory suggested in the authors' papers [J. Knot Theory Ramifications 18, No. 6, 791--823 (2009; Zbl 1189.57006) and Dokl. Math. 80, No. 2, 739--742 (2009); translation from Dokl. Akad. Nauk, Ross. Akad. Nauk 428, No. 5, 591--594 (2009; Zbl 1180.57012)], see also [\textit{L. Traldi} and \textit{L. Zulli}, J. Knot Theory Ramifications 18, No. 12, 1681--1709 (2009; Zbl 1204.57009)], dealing with a generalization of knots obtained by translating the Reidemeister moves for links into the language of intersection graphs of chord diagrams. In this paper we show how some methods of classical and virtual knot theory can be translated into the language of abstract graphs, and some theorems can be reproved and generalised to this graphical setting. We construct various invariants, prove certain minimality theorems and construct functorial mappings for graph-knots and graph-links. In this paper, we show for the first time the non-equivalence of some graph-links to virtual links.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1237.57001].

title.title: Studying complex manifolds by using groups \(G_n^k\) and \(\Gamma_n^k\)

editorial_contributions.text:
The authors study the irrationality function of a real number \(\alpha\), introduced by \[\psi_{\alpha}(t)=\min_{q\in\mathbb{Z}_{+},q\leq t}\,\|q\alpha\|,\text{ with }\|x\|=\min_{a\in\mathbb{Z}}\,|x-a|.\] In a paper by \textit{I. D. Kan} and \textit{N. G. Moshchevitin} [Unif. Distrib. Theory 5, No. 2, 79--86 (2010; Zbl 1249.11064)] it was shown that the difference \(\psi_{\alpha}(t)-\psi_{\beta}(t)\) for two irrational numbers changes sign infinitely often as \(t\rightarrow\infty\).

In this paper the authors give a generalization of this theorem to the case of \(n\geq 2\) real numbers.

An important quantity here is the so called \(k\)-index. Let \({\mathbf{a}}=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)\) be an \(n\)-tuple pairwise incommensurable numbers (i.e., \(\psi_{\alpha_i}(t)\not=\psi_{\alpha_j}(t)\) for \(i\not= j\) and all sufficiently large \(t\)).

Then there exists for all sufficiently large \(t\) a permutation \[\vec{\sigma}(t):\{1,2,3,\ldots,n\}\rightarrow \{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3,\ldots,\sigma_n\} \] with \[\psi_{\alpha_{\sigma_1}}(t) >\psi_{\alpha_{\sigma_2}}(t)>\psi_{\alpha_{\sigma_3}}(t)>\ldots>\psi_{\alpha_{\sigma_n}}(t).\] The \(k\)-index \(\mathbf{k(a)}=\mathbf{k}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)\) is now defined by \[{\mathbf{k(a)}}=\max\{k:\text{ exists } k\text{ permutations with }\sigma_j\ (1\leq j\leq k\text{ with }\text{ for all } j\text{ for all } t_0>0\] \[ \text{ exists } t>t_0\text{ with }\sigma(t)=\sigma_j\}.\] The main result of the paper is now:

Theorem 1. Let \({\mathbf{a}}=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)\) be an \(n\)-tuple pairwise incommensurable numbers, then \[\mathbf{k(a)}\geq \sqrt{\frac{n}{2}}.\]

Moreover, the following theorem shows that this result leads to the optimal number for the inequality:

Theorem 2. Let \(k\geq 3\) and \(n=\frac{(k(k+1)}{2}\), then there exists an \(n\)-tuple \(\mathbf{a}\) pairwise incommensurable numbers with \[\mathbf{k(a)}=k.\]

The layout of the paper is as follows:

\S1 The \(k\)-index.

Contains the main results.

\S2 Continued fractions.

\S3 The main Lemma (\(3\) pages).

\S4 Proof of Theorem 1 (\(2\frac{1}{2}\) pages).

\S5 Four numbers (\(1\) page).

\S6 Proof of Theorem 2 (\(3\) pages).

References (\(11\) items).

A nicely written paper.

title.title: Representations of \(G_n^3\) and related groups

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper is an introduction to a combinatorial theory arising as a natural generalization of classical and virtual knot theory.

The authors introduce a new class of objects closely connected to both classical and virtual knots, called graph-links. This class of objects is different from the one described by \textit{L. Traldi} and \textit{L. Zulli} [J. Knot Theory Ramifications 18, No.~12, 1681--1709; (2009; Zbl 1204.57009)]. To construct such an object, the authors define the intersection graph of a chord diagram, which is a labeled graph, i.e. a simple graph with vertices labeled with \(+\) or \(-\). Remember that a chord diagram is a cubic graph consisting of an oriented cycle and several non-oriented edges, called chords, connecting points on the cycle. A chord diagram is labeled if every chord is endowed with a sign \(+\) or \(-\). The intersection graph of a labeled chord diagram \(D\) is a labeled graph such that its vertices are in one-to-one correspondence with chords of \(D\), the label of a vertex corresponds to the label of the corresponding chord, and two vertices are connected by an edge if and only if the corresponding chords are linked. The authors then consider general simple labeled graphs and define graphs-moves corresponding to chord-moves. As a result a new object is obtained, an equivalence class of labeled graphs under formal moves. So a graph-link is an equivalence class of simple labeled graphs modulo the graph-moves.

The authors also construct an invariant Kauffman bracket and Jones polynomial corresponding to graph-links. This bracket counts the number of non-existing circles of a non-realizable chord diagram.

title.title: Introduction to graph-link theory

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: In this paper, we introduce \(\mathbb{Z}_2\)-braids and, more generally, \(G\)-braids for an arbitrary group \(G\). They form a natural group-theoretic counterpart of \(G\)-knots, see [\textit{V. O. Manturov}, J. Knot Theory Ramifications 24, No. 10, Article ID 1540006, 14 p. (2015; Zbl 1325.05157)]. The underlying idea used in the construction of these objects -- decoration of crossings with some additional information -- generalizes an important notion of \textit{parity} introduced by the second author (see [\textit{V. O. Manturov}, Sb. Math. 201, No. 5, 693--733 (2010; Zbl 1210.57010)]) to different combinatorically geometric theories, such as knot theory, braid theory and others. These objects act as natural enhancements of classical (Artin) braid groups. The notion of dotted braid group is introduced: classical (Artin) braid groups live inside dotted braid groups as those elements having presentation with no dots on the strands. The paper is concluded by a list of unsolved problems.

title.title: On marked braid groups

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: This paper considers \(\ast\)-graphs in which all vertices have degree 4 or 6, and studies the question of calculating the genus of nonorientable surfaces into which such graphs may be embedded. In a previous paper [the authors, J. Knot Theory Ramifications 22, No. 12, Article ID 1341005, 15 p. (2013; Zbl 1278.05083)] by the authors, the problem of calculating whether a given \(\ast\)-graph in which all vertices have degree 4 or 6 admits a \(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\)-homologically trivial embedding into a given orientable surface was shown to be equivalent to a problem on matrices. Here we extend those results to nonorientable surfaces. The embeddability condition that we obtain yields quadratic-time algorithms to determine whether a \(\ast\)-graph with all vertices of degree 4 or 6 admits a \(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\)-homologically trivial embedding into the projective plane or into the Klein bottle.
